articles.title: Joy, hope and anger as Serbia student movement’s political novices enter parliament
articles.summary: Celebrating supporters say they feel vindicated by arrival of Student List candidates in national assembly
body: The paved plateau in front of Serbia’s national assembly became an impromptu dancefloor, as people of all ages joyfully whirled in a kolo. Drivers passing by sounded their horns, while hundreds of people waved flags, blew whistles and cheered. Every now and again, the crowd parted, allowing smartly dressed men and women to walk up the steps and into the building.

These were the candidates from the Student List, on their way to being sworn in as members of parliament after their stunning victory in last month’s parliamentary elections. Those who had come to cheer them on displayed their feelings on badges, flags and placards.
Related: Serbia’s Student List candidates sworn in as MPs after election triumph

“Srećan rad” was a common sentiment – “Good luck with your work”. Another ubiquitous slogan revived the catchphrase of a politically ambitious young girl from a popular 1990s sitcom, Open Doors (Otvorena vrata) – “the assembly is starting”.

Tuesday’s delight echoed the euphoria of election night, when the Student List’s collection of political novices defeated the long-serving populist leader Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS).

A group from the Belgrade suburb of Zemun were among the crowd, including Lijlana, who was holding a sign reading: “What one person cannot do, 3 can” – a reference to the Student List’s number on the ballot papers.

“This is the voice of the people,” she said. “People who want peace, who want the government to do their job, who want to have institutions that are operating in favour of people, not in favour of the mafia.”
Her friend Jelena agreed. “This is an historic moment for Serbia,” she said.

Members of Serbia’s student movement were also on the assembly steps. They said they were feeling vindication that two years of youth-led protests had produced such a stunning result, and hopeful about the Student List’s prospects in government.

“We are celebrating winning against the regime of Aleksandar Vučić,” said Aleksandar, a political science student at Belgrade university. “I want the new government to make a better life for us,” added his classmate Iva.

But in some quarters, anger remains the dominant emotion. The protests were triggered by the deaths of 16 people after a canopy collapsed at a renovated railway station in Serbia’s second city, Novi Sad. The students blamed endemic corruption, and held Vučić and the SNS responsible.

Judging by some of the placards outside the assembly, forgiveness seems unlikely. One sign suggested that erstwhile SNS ministers should “end up like Elena and Nicolae Ceaușescu,” Romania’s former first couple, who were executed after a show trial in 1989.

In fact, most of the SNS members who arrived for the inaugural session faced nothing worse than jeers, with the exception of Lidija Vukićević. A woman in the crowd poured a bottle of drinking yoghurt over her head, prompting Vukićević to criticise the “primitivism and vulgarity” of Student List supporters. The incident also allowed Vučić to push his narrative that the students were promoting a regime of “naked terror” by targeting SNS members for harassment and arrest. All they could offer Serbia was “hatred and yoghurt”, he said.

The student movement was quick to condemn the incident, with one faculty group posting that it was “not in line with the values we stand for and fight for”. It urged supporters “to treat all fellow citizens peacefully and with dignity, regardless of their political affiliation”.

Inside the assembly, it did not take long for the new intake to be sworn in as MPs. Hundreds of journalists and photographers crammed into the debating chamber to witness the ceremony marking the end of 14 years of SNS government. It was a discombobulating experience for some, with Bojan Dimitrijević, who until recently was best known as an actor, needing to be reminded he was now an MP, rather than a candidate.

“In my theatre work we make illusions to illustrate some truths, but here we are making some realistic things that will change the imagination of the people,” said the 53-year-old, who worked with Samantha Morton and John Hurt in the TV series The Last Panthers. He said he was particularly concerned with culture and ecology, but conceded that he did not know “where to start with fixing every problem we have here”.

If nothing else, the Student List can call on expertise from a wide range of professions. Dimitrijević’s fellow MPs include the former basketball player Dejan Bodiroga, a high-school English teacher, Katarina Šćepanović, and Dejan Šoškić, a former governor of the National Bank of Serbia. Keen to get on with forming a government, they found themselves frustrated on their first day in the job by SNS delaying tactics.

Vučić, now in opposition, addressed the assembly for more than 90 minutes, while the acting speaker, Stojan Radenović, called regular extended breaks. The cardiologist Ilija Srdanović, who topped the Student List’s candidate list, said this was pointless and expensive, describing “every day of delay in decision-making” as “a burden on the citizens of Serbia”.
On the sunny plateau outside the building, small groups of Student List supporters seemed unfazed. Some of them had waited 14 years to see Vučić out of office.

Standing alongside her friends from Zemun, Jelena put it in perspective. “This is just the starting day of the democratic era in Serbia,” she said. The SNS can only delay; with a 30-seat working majority, the Student List now holds the power.

articles.title: Anti-Arab hate speech surged on social media during Israel’s election, report finds
articles.summary: Digital monitors recorded 400% rise in posts attacking Arab Israelis, including Netanyahu’s disproven fraud allegations
body: Anti-Arab hate speech surged on social media in Israel around the country’s general election last month, digital monitors have said, as politicians including Benjamin Netanyahu levelled disproven allegations against Arab Israeli parties of election fraud.

A new report by the Israel-based Brandeis Institute and FakeReporter recorded a deluge of anti-Arab discourse across social media platforms such as X, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok in the days surrounding Israel’s 27 October election.
According to FakeReporter’s analysis, anti-Arab sentiment on X rose by more than 400% from election day on 27 October to 29 October. Similar content also spread across Facebook and other platforms.

Arab-majority parties won 19 seats in the Israeli Knesset in last month’s election, potentially putting them in a kingmaker position. The opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been invited to try to put together a coalition to replace Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist government.

The posts mainly pushed three messages, the first of which was the allegation that “the Arabs stole the election” via fraud, vote buying and foreign interference, according to the report. Israel’s electoral commission had already publicly refuted such claims.
Posts also depicted Arab citizens of Israel as a security threat and called for them to have their right to vote restricted.

Some of the most-viewed posts also came from top Israeli officials and Netanyahu’s post “They stole the election in Israel!” was viewed 1.2m times. A post by the far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, calling for heads of Arab political parties was also viewed more than 350,000 times.

FakeReporter said much of the anti-Arab hate speech was fuelled by politicians from Netanyahu’s political bloc. “It can be said that they were a major factor in spreading hate speech against Arab citizens of Israel following the election,” its analysis said.

Arab citizens of Israel, the majority of whom are Palestinians, make up 21% of the population of Israel. Since the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack and Israel’s subsequent war in Gaza, Arab political leaders have faced increasingly inflammatory attacks and accusations of dual loyalties.

In the run-up to the election, Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted to bar the country’s two main Arab majority political lists from running – a move later struck down by the Israeli supreme court.
Eisenkot last week condemned what he called a “racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation” against the country’s Arab citizens.

The Brandeis Institute and FakeReporter sent letters to Google, Meta, TikTok and X on 4 November calling on them to take steps to stop the proliferation of hate speech against Arab citizens of Israel on their platforms.

Only Google responded, saying that Israel’s election is a “Priority 0” for the company and that it has dedicated resources to monitoring traffic around the election, but that the Central Elections Committee had made no requests for extra moderation procedures.

articles.title: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule
articles.summary: With the SpaceX satellite system faltering, Ukraine’s military launched a surprise, multi-pronged attack to take down vital bridge to Crimea
body: At 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south.

Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions.

“We knew what the target was. Everyone was enthusiastic and excited,” one person who took part in the special operation, using the pseudonym “Leon”, told the Guardian. His 7th Deep Strike Centre is part of “Magyar’s Birds”, a brigade named after the call sign of its founder, Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces. Leon said: “Nobody gets excited any more about oil refineries. This was different.”
The soldiers got ready to launch, then watched the biplane-like drone, laden with explosives, disappear across the southern Ukrainian steppe.

Over the next four hours, hundreds of attack drones followed the same linear path, flying first over land and then over the Black Sea. In the early hours of the morning they arrived at their destination: the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia. Putin opened the monumental road and rail crossing in 2018, driving across it in a Kamaz truck. This was four years after his undercover troops – known as little green men – seized the peninsula.

Russian propagandists had described the bridge as impregnable. It was, they said, an edifice as strong and unyielding as their country’s iron leader. For Ukraine, by contrast, it was a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Also, officials pointed out, it was illegal. Twice Kyiv had tried to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.

On this occasion, the Ukrainian military’s careful, multi-stage plan worked perfectly. “It was a well-coordinated operation. Waves of drones started from different locations. The goal was to overwhelm Russia’s well-organised air defence system, rather than the bridge itself,” Leon explained.

As expected, the initial salvo tied up Russia’s local defences. According to insiders, Ukraine then launched a second drone wave. Its function was crucial and different: to act as a relay system for radio signals. Previously, Ukrainian units had used Starshield, the military equivalent of Starlink, for mid-range strikes on occupied territory. Elon Musk’s SpaceX owns the satellite internet network, which is overseen by the Pentagon and the Trump administration.

Ten days ago, however, limits were mysteriously imposed on Ukrainian drones, so they could no longer fly at above 161 km/h (100 mph). SpaceX insists there is no slowdown – a statement Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says is untrue. On Monday night, it appears Kyiv bypassed US restrictions by setting up its own extraordinary and innovative real-time video and radio connection.

Once the relay was in place, a third wave of attacks could begin. This time they featured Flamingos, a potent Ukrainian-made cruise missile capable of carrying 1,000kg of explosives – enough to seriously damage the bridge. An unknown number of missiles – some reports say at least four – were launched from southern Ukraine and sent towards Crimea.

A video from one of the Flamingos shows it drawing inexorably towards the target. The onboard camera captures a ghostly night-time scene. The crossing looms into view against a grisaille background. Suddenly a gigantic steel arch appears. The feed cuts out. Other footage shows the moment of impact: an orange fireball, pricking the surrounding blackness.

Photos taken on Tuesday morning in the aftermath of the attack show a scene of watery devastation. A massive arch had tumbled overnight into the Kerch straight, with a large concrete chunk of the road crossing. Nobody will be driving across the bridge anytime soon. The adjacent railway arch span was also damaged. “We were very happy, swapping messages all night,” Leon said.

One source in Ukraine’s armed forces said the timing of the operation – hailed by Zelenskyy as “unprecedented” – was deliberate. It was conducted ahead of a meeting on Thursday between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of an Apec summit. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.

They added: “We understand that what we did shows the world that the king is nude. Putin is weak and vulnerable and we just proved it. The operation was purposefully designed for this specific historic moment. Putin’s plan was to bluff at the summit about how powerful he is. In reality, he can’t even protect the most important and symbolic pillars of his regime.”

In addition to Putin’s political embarrassment before his peers, the disabling of the Kerch bridge has practical consequences. Since annexing Crimea, Russia has militarised the peninsula, effectively turning it into a giant and fortified army base. Since 2022 it has been used as a launch platform for drone and missile attacks on the port of Odesa, and other Ukrainian cities in the region.

Russia’s occupying southern army has relied on the bridge for regular deliveries of ammunition, equipment and fuel. With the crossing partially closed – rail travel reportedly reopened on Tuesday – Russia will have to use an under fire land corridor instead, connecting its Rostov oblast with the Moscow-controlled parts of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces.

“We have disrupted their logistics to Crimea. There will be a lot of problems for Russia’s army in the south,” Leon predicted. Debris from the bridge strike is obstructing the narrow shipping corridor through the Kerch strait, linking the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. The Azov sea now resembles a lake. Passenger ferries are unable to move, with the occupied ports of Mariupol and Berdyansk cut off.

The soldiers returned from their mission jubilant and elated. Back at their headquarters, they gathered as usual for a minute’s silence, in memory of those killed in Russia’s bloody war. “We had our daily ritual as usual. Then there were congratulations on a very successful and important operation,” Leon said. Then he added: “We are paying them back.”
• Luke Harding’s Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest is published by Guardian Faber. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

articles.title: ‘They were keeping it for a rainy day’: Ukraine’s Kerch bridge attack is proof Kyiv still has cards to play
articles.summary: Partial demolition of bridge linking Russia and occupied Crimea is obvious embarrassment to Putin days before meeting with Xi and Trump
body: Ukraine’s attack on the Kerch road bridge overnight is the culmination of weeks, and perhaps months, of military operations plus years of industrial development, during which Kyiv has developed its own cruise missiles and long-range drones.

The demolition is not quite total, because the rail bridge is still standing, one line in operation – but the attack is an obvious embarrassment to Russia two days before Vladimir Putin is due to meet Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.

Such is the collapse of a span of the roadway, and the loss of its supporting arch above, it appears to be a level of damage that “cannot be repaired any time soon”, says Ben Hodges, a former commanding general of the US army in Europe.

The 19km (12-mile), $3.6bn (£2.7bn) road bridge connecting Russia to the east of Crimea was completed in 2018, a project closely associated with Putin and his efforts to secure the 2014 annexation of Crimea by opening up a supply route to the peninsula.

Russia’s leader was filmed driving an orange truck into Crimea, greeted by cheering workers once the construction was complete. “Putin initiated this project himself,” the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said at the time.

That was four years before Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which has, if anything, made Russia’s position in Crimea more precarious, though the change in the balance of power is a while coming.
Russia was able to bomb anywhere in Ukraine in 2022, while Kyiv was denied long-range western missiles, particularly those powerful enough to strike such a politically sensitive and strategic target.

Instead, Ukraine tried to blow the bridge up with a truck bomb in 2022 and a sea drone attack a year later. Neither did much long-term damage. It was only as Ukraine’s own long-range drones and cruise missiles came to fruition near the beginning of 2026 that a knockout strike became possible.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that the culminating attacks on the bridge, the end of two days of strikes, involved Ukrainian-made Neptune and Flamingo FP-5 cruise missiles, Palianytsia rocket drones plus Ruta cruise missiles from the Dutch manufacturer Destinus, the only foreign arms company confirmed as involved.

It was, the Ukrainian president said, the “seventh stage” in an operation “carried out over several weeks”. Radars, jamming equipment and air defence systems were progressively neutralised, opening up corridors of attack.

Meanwhile, Russia had already started what is becoming a battle of the bridges. Moscow attacked Kyiv’s busy Northern and Southern bridges in early October, part of its scaled-up campaign against the capital and the country’s other large cities.

Russia is struggling to make progress on the frontline, and a record 50,000 troops were killed or seriously wounded in October, according to the Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte. Its efforts are focused on knocking out Ukraine’s electricity, heating and water supplies, though attacking bridges show its target list is expanding in grim desperation.

Yet the Kremlin has chosen this expansion at a time when Ukraine can strike back. The pro-war Russian military blogger Military Informant notes that Ukraine has a “parity in firepower”, having downed the Kerch road bridge in two days of air raids. “It cannot be ruled out that the railway section will be destroyed next,” the blogger adds.

If anything, further attacks on the bridge are almost certain both to prevent its repair and to make resupplying Crimea more difficult. Cutting the bridge entirely, rail and road, would leave Moscow with only the R-280 land highway from Rostov to Crimea, already the subject of months of Ukrainian drone attacks.

Hodges has long argued that Crimea could be a defining theatre of the war, because “of what Crimea represents to Putin”. Ukraine should try to make “Russian occupation untenable” by destroying the bridge and asserting fire control over the R-280, he adds.

A supply squeeze, however, is a slow process, though its political benefits may be felt more quickly. Bringing down the road bridge “further kills the narrative that Russian victory is inevitable or that Crimea is theirs”, Hodges says, although Trump may not bring up the episode in his meeting with Putin and Xi on Thursday.

The danger is that both sides, in their desperation to end a deadlocked war, will escalate further. However, cut out of the talks in Shenzen, Zelenskyy had little choice but to remind Trump as well as Putin that Ukraine still has cards to play.

Emily Ferris, a Russia expert with the Rusi thinktank, says Ukraine’s military-industrial complex was ready for some months, meaning the timing of the attack on the Kerch bridge can be interpreted only as political.
“They were keeping it for a rainy day, and that day has come,” she said.

articles.title: What is the polar vortex, why has it flipped and will it bring the UK snow?
articles.summary: We look at what is happening over the Arctic and what it might mean for winter weather in the northern hemisphere
body: The polar vortex has flipped direction, signalling the earliest “major sudden stratospheric warming” ever observed. We examine how it is likely to affect you and whether it will bring snow.

It is a circle of strong winds in the stratosphere, about six to 30 miles (10 to 50km) above the surface of the Earth, that usually blow in a west to east direction around the Arctic, creating an insulating ring between the cold air mass closer to the north pole and warmer air further south.
The vortex relocates or splits in two, which allows cold air from high altitudes and the pole to spill down over northern Europe, north America, Siberia, Japan and other parts of east Asia.

This part of the stratosphere is thought to have warmed by up to 50C in just a couple of days as a result of large atmospheric waves spreading up from the troposphere, the lowest and densest layer of Earth’s atmosphere.
Not always, but in this case, yes, for at least some parts of the northern hemisphere in the coming weeks.
The polar vortex is part of the climate system. Any disruption has knock-on effects. In the north Atlantic, for example, it upsets the jet stream and weather patterns for millions of people.

When the jet stream is weakened or wobbles, chilled air can move south out of the Arctic, often bringing colder, drier spells to northern Europe and north America, while southern Europe tends to become milder, wetter and windier.

Very possibly, but it’s not guaranteed. It depends where high pressure systems form. The UK Met Office released a yellow snow warning on Tuesday for the Midlands, the north east and west of England and south west Scotland.

Yes, sudden stratospheric warming famously led a few weeks later to “the beast from the east” snowstorms that affected the UK in 2018. In the US, it was associated with deadly winter storms in 2021. Similar phenomena were also observed in 2009-10 and 2013. These events usually occur much later in winter, but this year it has happened on 10 November, 18 days earlier than ever before.
The probability of colder-than-average weather tends to continue for between 30 and 40 days after sudden stratospheric warming.

This is a matter for debate, but scientists have found evidence that El Niño conditions, which start with warmer waters in the Pacific, influence planetary waves – known as Rossby waves – that spread across the lower atmosphere and can propagate upwards in the Arctic, raising the chance of sudden stratospheric warming.

Possibly, but the scientific jury is still out. Some researchers say a link is likely. Others are more cautious, noting that early sudden stratospheric warming falls within the bounds of natural variability. Even though this event comes at the end of a year of extreme weather, the bigger question is likely to be filed under “more study is needed”.

articles.title: Trump claims US is ‘looking into’ Iranian bomb plot in Washington despite ‘no credible threats’
articles.summary: US officials ‘debate whether Iran can or will attempt to execute’ plot to detonate a ‘dirty bomb’, report says
body: Donald Trump has claimed the US is “looking into” whether Iran is developing plans to detonate a so-called “dirty bomb” in Washington, even as the White House said there were “no credible threats” at this time.
Trump said his administration takes the idea “very seriously”

After a CNN report, citing seven unnamed US officials, that new US intelligence suggested Iran was working on plans that would use a dirty bomb, which combines conventional explosives with radioactive material, or a chemical weapon against senior Trump administration officials.
The report noted, however, that US officials “continue to debate whether Iran can or will attempt to execute such a plot”.

The US president’s war on Iran is deeply unpopular among Americans. His Republican party was widely rejected by voters in the midterm elections, in which the GOP lost control of the Senate and House of Representatives.

Asked in the Philippines on Tuesday if there was reason to believe that such an Iranian attack was imminent, Trump said: “If there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before. I hope it’s not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to ​be crazy.”
Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement: “We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland.”

CNN cited the unnamed officials as saying that Tehran’s planning was an effort by Iran to “give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack”, but the plans include specific locations and targets.
While the plans would signify that Iran is willing to escalate its tactics against the US, there is no evidence to suggest they will go ahead with them.

The US and Israel went to war with Iran starting in February, with early airstrikes killing Iranian officials, including the supreme leader, Ali Khamenei. Trump has repeatedly claimed the war will be over soon, but it has continued.

The US president has argued that US involvement in the war is necessary so that the country does not build nuclear weapons. Iran has blocked trade through the strait of Hormuz, creating rising fuel costs – and rattling the global economy.

articles.title: Australia’s gender pay gap falls below 20% for first time
articles.summary: Men still dominate top-paid positions but businesses’ ‘deliberate’ decisions have narrowed gap, workplace gender equality agency report finds
body: Australian women earn 80c for every $1 men earn, on average, after Australia’s gender pay gap fell below 20% for the first time in 2025-26.
The workplace gender equality agency’s (WGEA) report on Wednesday showed men still dominated top-paid positions but businesses’ decisions have narrowed the gap.

WGEA chief Christine Castley said most Australian employers were ignoring backlash to diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) and improving their hiring and promotion to ensure women reached senior positions.
“Employers are actually thinking in a very deliberate way about what’s going on with workplace gender equality and then taking action,” Castley told Guardian Australia.
The overall WGEA pay gap was 19.7% for the year, with the 2025-26 survey including federal government public sector employers for the first time.
The figure has improved significantly in the last decade, from 26.3% in 2015-16. Coverage has also increased, now covering more than 6m employees across 9,096 employers.
The private sector’s pay gap fell from 21.1% last year to 20.3% this year, as women accounted for a growing share of full-time management and leadership roles.
Bigger pay rises in female-dominated industries, including retail, aged care and childcare, also helped narrow the gap.
However, women-dominated industries and occupations were still typically paid less than those dominated by men. The average woman still earned $27,467 less per year than the average man, WGEA found.
The survey accounted not only for wages but all earnings, including penalty rates, superannuation, bonuses and overtime. Average total remuneration in the survey was $125,568.
The overall distribution of pay did not improve from 2024-25. Women make up about half of Australia’s workforce but men remained overrepresented in the highest-paid positions.
Every level of management was dominated by men, WGEA found. The disparity was greatest at the chief executive level, where three in four CEOs were men and the gender pay gap widened to 27.6%.

Women accounted for just 36% of employees in the top pay quartile in the private sector. In the commonwealth public sector, women’s representation in the top quartile was 46% and the gender pay gap was just 7.8%.

Promotion rates are similar between genders but women are less represented at higher levels, likely because they resign or take time off for care and domestic responsibilities, previous WGEA work has found.
Wednesday’s report found just 7% of manager roles are part-time, but 29% of women work part-time compared with 12% of men. WGEA called for workplaces to redesign roles to allow more part-time work.
In the financial services sector, which has the worst pay gap at 26.7%, men would be more likely to be promoted or get bonuses as they took on more visible work, Castley said.

“[It’s] the person who can attend the client functions [and] can be available 24/7, the person who’s most visible to the leadership of the organisation, versus, perhaps, the person [doing] the work that’s behind the scenes,” Castley said.
Superannuation provider Rest was an outlier in the finance industry. Its pay gap has fallen to 9.4%, from 20.1% in 2022.

Rest’s chief people officer, Amy Murrell, said the improvements had been helped by extending paid parental leave to all permanent staff, regardless of gender, time of arrival or primary or secondary carer classification.
“It’s not going to happen naturally,” Murrell said. “I think you have to prioritise it for it to make sense.”
The firm had also increased representation after setting targets for at least 40% of employees to be women and 40% men at every level of its business, from its board to its investment team.

Castley said some Australian business leaders had taken on an “anti-DEI” narrative, amid global backlash to diversity, equity and inclusion measures, but most businesses were “getting on with the job”.

WGEA asked businesses to set new targets for the first time in 2026. The most popular goals included improving gender balance at junior and managerial levels and consulting employees on gender equality efforts.

“These are the real issues that need to be tackled … and it’s actually very reassuring that those are the targets that employers have picked because it demonstrates, I think, a very real commitment to actually taking action,” Castley said.

articles.title: Ukraine critically damages Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia
articles.summary: Zelenskyy praises ‘unprecedented attack’ but Kremlin claims bridge will be restored and will be ‘better than ever’
body: Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed as an “unprecedented” military operation.

Footage showed a Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile seconds before it hit the road and railway crossing, followed by an explosion. The strike follows an earlier attack on Monday that targeted an arch across its central section.

Writing on social media, the Ukrainian president described the attack as “a response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure”. He said it was the culmination of a long and complex campaign to demolish the bridge, involving domestically produced drones and ballistic missiles. Palianytsia drones hit the road section of the bridge, while Neptune and other missiles targeted the adjacent rail section, he added.

The Ukrainian general staff said an arch and a span of the bridge’s road section had collapsed, severing the road link, while the railway line was still standing but its arch was damaged. Train travel across the bridge resumed on Tuesday after a brief pause.

Earlier, Russian forces had struck ⁠two major bridges in Kyiv that straddle the Dnipro River late on Monday, along with some other critical infrastructure, amid drone ⁠and missile attacks ​across Ukraine.

Ukraine has declared that the Kerch bridge, built eight years ago after Vladimir Putin’s 2014 annexation of Crimea and known officially as the Crimean Bridge, is illegal. It has repeatedly attempted to destroy it, using a truck bomb in 2022 and a sea drone strike the following year.
The latest drone and missile barrage appears to have succeeded after months in which Ukrainian unmanned systems forces have systematically knocked out the peninsula’s multi-layered air defences.

A Ukrainian military source said the operation was timed to embarrass Putin before his meeting on Thursday with Xi Jinping and Donald Trump in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. The three leaders are attending an Apec summit. “Putin looks weak and vulnerable. He can’t protect the most important and symbolic pillars of his regime,” the source said.

The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed that road traffic on the bridge had been suspended. “We ask residents and visitors in Crimea to refrain from travelling toward the bridge and to take these restrictions into account when planning their routes,” he posted on Telegram.

Photos on Tuesday suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea. The adjacent railway arch span has also sustained damage.

Ukrainian commentators say the massive steel arch cannot easily be replaced. The closure of the bridge means traffic from Crimea can travel out of the peninsula only via a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, vulnerable to Ukrainian drones.

The debris appears to have blocked the main navigable route beneath the bridge, used by maritime traffic from the Sea of Azov and the ports of Berdiansk and Mariupol. The channel is 120 metres wide and 8.3 metres deep. Submerged steel struts could prevent large vessels from passing until the debris is removed.

The Russian government convened an emergency meeting to assess the attack, according to the Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov. Peskov added that the bridge would be repaired and would be “even better than before”, in comments to the Russian newspaper Izvestia.

But pro-war Russian commentators acknowledged that repairing the bridge would be very difficult, warning that, unlike in 2022 and 2023, Ukraine now had the capability to strike floating cranes and repair crews.
“Even installing a prefabricated arch under such conditions would be a formidable challenge,” wrote the influential Rybar Telegram channel, with close links to the defence ministry.

Ukrainian observers were gleeful at the bridge’s long-awaited destruction. They also pointed out that Ukraine’s armed forces could hit the bridge again to prevent repair work from being carried out. Serhii Sternenko, a former adviser to the defence ministry in Kyiv, wrote: “In response to your many questions. Yes, the bridge is fucked.”

The Ukrainian blogger Anton Gerashchenko pointed out that Putin personally opened the bridge in 2018, driving across it in a Kamaz truck. “The Kerch bridge stands as the primary symbol of the Russian occupation of Ukrainian Crimea and the embodiment of its illegal annexation. It is Putin’s flagship project,” he wrote.

He added: “For years, Russian authorities claimed the bridge was ‘the most protected facility in the world’. Consequently, every successful strike shatters the myth of the invincibility of Russian air defences – as well as the notion that Ukraine is incapable of reaching key targets deep behind enemy lines.”

Ukrainians celebrated on Tuesday with memes. The company Fire Point, which manufactures the Flamingo missile, posted a popcorn emoji. Other social media users shared video of “Kerch Bridge on Fire”, a popular song by Saint Javelin which has become an anti-Moscow anthem.

Russian military bloggers were gloomy. One, Russian Engineer, acknowledged the Ukrainian military operation to paralyse the bridge had been “perfect”. Hundreds of unmanned aerial vehicles distracted Russian air defences, he said, before a clinical strike by ballistic missiles.
The attack will further complicate supplies to Crimea, after a summer in which the peninsula struggled with fuel shortages and an intensifying Ukrainian campaign to isolate it from mainland Russia.

Ukraine has for months focused its strikes on the key transport routes supplying Crimea, particularly the so-called Novorossiya highway, a key logistics corridor linking the peninsula to Russia’s Rostov region through the occupied cities of Melitopol and Mariupol.

Russia had already sharply restricted traffic across the Crimean Bridge. Moscow has largely stopped using the crossing for rail fuel shipments since the 2022 Ukrainian attack damaged the bridge and set a fuel train ablaze.

Rybar wrote that the latest strike would force Moscow to “completely overhaul” its supply routes to Crimea, shifting more traffic to the Novorossiya highway. Russia would also have to step up the installation of protective netting along the route, Rybar added, lamenting that the measure had not been introduced in the spring.

Meanwhile, in Kyiv loud explosions could be heard as Russian forces struck two bridges over the Dnipro River. The mayor of the Ukrainian capital, Vitali Klitschko, wrote on Telegram that according to “preliminary information, there have been hits on the north and south bridges in ⁠the capital”. There were water and power cuts in parts of the city, he added later.
Russian forces launched a ​series of attacks on bridges crossing ‌the river earlier this ‌month and in October.
A Russian missile attack injured three people ‌in the region of Cherkasy and also targeted Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second biggest city, local officials said on Telegram.

Russia’s defence ministry claimed ⁠on ⁠Tuesday its ​forces had ⁠carried out a massive ⁠overnight strike ​on ‌Ukrainian ‌military-industrial facilities, ‌transport infrastructure in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia and the ‌Cherkasy and Dnipropetrovsk regions.
The ministry ​said the strikes also ⁠targeted energy facilities, ​port infrastructure ​and ​vessels ​used ‌by ​Ukraine’s armed ​forces.
Russian defence ministry data from Monday showed that an overnight Ukrainian drone barrage was the biggest since the start of full-scale war in 2022.

Zelenskyy also said on Monday ⁠that Ukraine had held new online talks with the US presidential envoys ​Steve Witkoff and ​Jared Kushner, as well as European ​representatives, on the prospects of ending the war with Russia.

Kushner ​said progress had been ‌made towards an ​agreement, though important ​challenges remain to end the war, which Russia started by invading Ukraine in February 2022. Moscow annexed the Black Sea Crimea peninsula in 2014.

articles.title: Serbia’s Student List candidates sworn in as MPs after election triumph
articles.summary: Inaugural parliamentary session comes as ousted populist Aleksandar Vučić threatens mass protests of his own
body: Candidates for Serbia’s Student List, the grassroots movement of political outsiders that pulled off a spectacular victory in last month’s elections over the party of the populist leader Aleksandar Vučić, have been sworn in as MPs as they begin the process of forming a government.

The 140 candidates – among them academics, lawyers, scientists and the odd actor – were sworn in on Tuesday during the inaugural session of the new parliament, bringing 14 years of rule by Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) to an end.

Before the parliamentary session, Student List supporters gathered outside the National Assembly to cheer their representatives. Some of them performed the traditional kolo circle dance in celebration.
Meanwhile, there were jeers and whistles for arrivals from Vučić’s party. A woman in the crowd poured a bottle of drinking yoghurt over the head of the SNS candidate Lidija Vukićević.

A caretaker government under the outgoing prime minister, Ðjuro Macut, will remain in office until MPs approve the Student List’s choice of a cabinet. For now, its makeup – including the identity of a future prime minister – remains unclear.

Sarah El Sarag, a human rights lawyer and MP-elect, said the wider student movement continued to be active in the process of selecting the cabinet, along with the candidates themselves. “We are there because of them,” she said of the students. “All the time, we are doing it together.”

Parliamentary planning sessions had helped prepare the candidates, she said. “We have been having meetings and exercises for the parliament almost every day, because none of us are professional politicians. We are lawyers, doctors, professors – and it is the first time for us to do this kind of job.”

The sessions reflect the Student List’s efforts to pre-empt sceptics who question whether a group of candidates with no political experience is equipped to govern. Members of the movement that selected El Sarag and her fellow MPs have reiterated that all are experts in their professional or academic fields and are better qualified than many of the people who served as ministers or MPs under Vučić.

El Sarag said her colleagues had a good idea of what to expect from Tuesday’s opening session. “People who have had some experience of politics have been making some simulated exercises for us,” she said.
She would not divulge the identity of the candidate for speaker – who will become Serbia’s acting president – let alone the name of the next prime minister.
Related: ‘A global political awakening’: how gen Z protests are sweeping the world

Vučić is not accepting his new role as leader of the opposition meekly. Since the election, he has accused the Student List of instituting a regime of “naked terror” by directing “submissive prosecutors and police” to carry out unlawful detentions.

Police and prosecutors have made a series of arrests of people with links to the SNS. Last week, prosecutors targeted the owners of a well-connected construction company over a project on the site of the once-famous Hotel Jugoslavija, which was hit during the 1999 Nato airstrikes on Belgrade.

That followed the arrest of the owner of Alta Bank, which held the concession for processing bill payments on behalf of Serbia’s state-owned electricity company. Others facing charges include senior police officers accused of abuse of office, and people suspected of vote rigging and violence during the elections.
After the two years of protests which culminated in the SNS’s defeat at the ballot box, Vučić is threatening major protests of his own.
Raša Nedeljkov, the programme director of the Serbian election and democracy monitor CRTA, said the first disruptions could come during parliament’s inaugural session.

“We can expect a lot of sabotage, a lot of obstruction, a lot of circus-creating atmosphere,” he said. “If we see such scenes in parliament – including some kind of physical obstruction – that’s something which would not surprise me.”

In such an atmosphere, speed may be of the essence, he said. MPs must approve a new cabinet within 90 days of the national assembly’s inaugural session but will be motivated to name a PM well before that deadline.

articles.title: Ed Miliband announces first sanctions on Israeli firms working in West Bank
articles.summary: Move is designed to hinder building of more illegal settlements, which Foreign Office says Israel has ‘refused to clamp down on’
body: Ed Miliband has announced the first set of sanctions against Israeli companies planning to build illegal settlements in the West Bank, after he pledged to try to prevent settlements that destroy the chances of a two-state solution.
The UK foreign secretary also announced he was placing sanctions on a rightwing activist Israeli group involved in trying to block aid into Gaza as recently as last month.

Miliband announced the measures just before tenders for the large E1 West Bank settlement were due to be allocated by the Israeli government, while saying he wanted to work with a new Israeli government in a more cooperative way.
Israel’s possible new prime minister, Gadi Eisenkot has said that, if appointed, he will take a tougher approach than Benjamin Netanyahu to settler violence.

The sanctions are designed to stop the flow of finance to eight identified construction firms, although in practice the extent to which any of the firms are dependent on British finance is yet to be tested.

On 8 September, Miliband announced an expansion of its Global Human Rights sanctions regime, as well as a complex set of measures, yet to be implemented, designed to ban the trade in goods from illegal settlements. The Foreign Office said that it welcomed and encouraged trade with “green line Israel” and firmly distinguished this with activity in settlements.

The Foreign Office said the current Israeli government had “not only refused to clamp down on illegal settlement, but has facilitated and encouraged them”. More settlements had been approved under the four years of this Israeli government than in the previous 20 years.

The entities targeted by sanctions are Israeli construction, property development and architectural businesses that have helped to plan, build, supply or market housing and public infrastructure in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Miliband – who was criticised by some for broadening the sanctions criteria and planning a ban on trade with illegal settlement – said: “Protecting the two-state solution is the north star of this government’s approach.

“That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution. And we will not stand by while those blocking desperately needed aid deepen the intolerable suffering of civilians in Gaza. The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable.”
Related: ‘The cold is lethal’: storms leave thousands in Gaza without shelter

But he added in a potential olive branch: “We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike.”

Miliband and his Middle East minister, Stephen Doughty, have repeatedly highlighted the Israeli government’s refusal to let a variety of dual-use goods into Gaza. The Foreign Office said civilians in Gaza were in desperate need of winter supplies, with catastrophic floods leaving nearly 4,000 households without shelter and 1.4 million people living in tents or makeshift shelters.

According to the UN, more than 150,000 tents and 300,000 tarpaulins bought by humanitarian partners and donors are outside Gaza ready to go in, but are being held by the Israeli authorities. The Israeli authorities also continue to block timber from entering, leaving no emergency shelter kits available in Gaza.

The Israeli government claims the blockage of some goods is necessary to prevent Hamas obtaining items that could be used to attack Israel. The dispute over dual-use goods and closed entry points into Gaza has lasted for more than two years.

articles.title: Hi-tech Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit
articles.summary: Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy
body: In a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping, is basking in its neon glow.

On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.

The broader Apec summit, meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.

All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.
A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.

“[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message. It’s a showcase of Chinese technological and economic achievements, and of China’s claim that it offers opportunities for prosperity in a world increasingly characterised by uncertainty and conflict.”

Like the light show, the summit is being carefully coordinated. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter as saying it would be one of the most tightly controlled in the organisation’s history, with leaders having to travel to a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park to meet Xi. The paper said diplomats had grumbled that the format “seems designed to reduce the free-flowing discussion characteristic of prior editions”.
Setting out its expectations for the summit, China’s foreign ministry has said it looks forward to “practical results in key areas such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, AI and so on”.

Already, Xi has announced trade wins with Canada’s Mark Carney, extending remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.

A meeting with Papua New ⁠Guinea’s leader, meanwhile, showed how Beijing’s geopolitical priorities have been absorbed and reflected by its allies, with James Marape recounting to Xi how he had closed Taiwan’s office in his country despite domestic challenges in doing so.

The most important meeting will be between Xi and Trump. The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are expected to tackle a broad range of issues including AI and trade. In a move that could strain the fragile tariff truce that the two leaders first agreed last year, the Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips.

Christopher Adams, a senior adviser at the law firm Covington who was at the centre of trade negotiations with China for the Obama and first Trump administrations, said: “The trade truce may increasingly look like a ceasefire in a war where major combat operations remain on hold but skirmishes are escalating to the point where the line between peace and war is blurred.
“I don’t see pressure to announce a further extension of the trade truce in Shenzhen. If a significant extension is announced, that would be an upside surprise.”

China has not hesitated to leverage Apec’s multinational platform in service of its arguments. A commentary by the state news agency Xinhua on Tuesday said: “Amid deepening geopolitical rivalries and growing global divisions, [China’s hosting] sends a clear signal that great-power competition need not be a zero-sum game, and that one country’s development need not come at the expense of another.”

The chair of the Apec senior officials’ meeting, Chen Xu, said Beijing had made trade “openness” a key focus of its Apec year and looked forward to “achieving more practical outcomes on the trade front”.

The much anticipated trilateral summit with Trump and Putin, on the other hand, could prove largely symbolic. For Xi, “it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States,” said Dr Kevork Oskanian, an expert on Russia at the University of Exeter. “Agreement on substantial issues, which would, in any case, require extensive preparatory negotiations, is unlikely.”

For China’s ruling Communist party, the political pomp has another key purpose. Nordin said summits were “occasions for leaders to tell stories about the world, about their country’s place in it … and one of the most important audiences for those stories is at home.”

For the locals watching the skyscraper light show on Monday night, the symbolism was not lost. China’s export might had helped it become increasingly powerful on the world stage, said one local man, who did not give his name. “It’s so great that the summit will take place in Shenzhen,” he said. “I feel very proud.”

articles.title: Hundreds arrested in anti-Trump protests in Philippines amid anger over Iran war and AI pact
articles.summary: Organisers say up to 10,000 people could join next round of demonstrations as US president arrives for Asean summit
body: Hundreds of people have been arrested in heated demonstrations against Donald Trump in Manila, as the US president arrived in the city for a leaders’ summit.

Organisers claimed as many as 10,000 people would be joining protests against Trump in the capital of the Philippines on Tuesday, where he is attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit. The crowds were expected to try to march to the summit site.
Related: Xi, Trump and Putin to discuss ‘world peace’ at trilateral, says China
Authorities have arrested nearly 300 people in widespread protests held in the days leading up to the summit, with large parts of the capital closed off and tight security in place.
Some burned effigies of Trump and faced off with police officers armed with batons and shields. Slogans on placards called the American leader the world’s “No 1 terrorist” in protests held on Monday.

Demonstrators angry at the cost of living and energy shock caused by the Iran war, and the new US-led Pax Silica initiative on AI and critical minerals, tried to reach the summit at the Philippine International Convention Center on Monday, but were blocked by police.

Pax Silica has sparked tensions in the Philippines over plans to build a tech hub outside Manila that critics say will affect water and energy supplies, and displace members of the Ayta Indigenous community.
Large sections of central Manila were closed to the public as part of the security cordon and public holidays put in place for the Asean summit.
After departing from Fairbanks in Alaska, Trump emerged from Air Force One at Ninoy Aquino International airport at 5.54pm local time (0954 GMT), live video showed.

Trump will meet with the leaders of Australia, Japan and India on Tuesday night before heading to Shenzhen in China on Wednesday. There he will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and hold trilateral talks with China’s president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.

The backlash against Trump follows the ousting of the boss of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, and allegations members of the US administration, including the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, knew about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump’s delegation was expected to include Elon Musk.

Protest leader Renato Reyes blamed the arrests in Manila on the heavy handed response of the government on the president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr, calling Monday the largest single day of police arrests since Marcos came to office in 2022.

“It is really crazy that the Philippine government is rolling out the red carpet for someone who has been so flatly rejected by the American people,” Reyes said. “Trump started a war that devastated the global economy and pushed oil prices in the Philippines to historic highs. It has caused untold suffering on the Filipino people.
“So, yes, Trump will have to pay for his crimes and he will have to be answerable, not just to the American people, but to the people of the world.”
The Philippine national police said some officers were injured during confrontations with demonstrators opposed to the summit, including when objects were allegedly thrown at officers.
Pax Silica will include a technology hub planned at New Clark City in Tarlac, about 100km from Manila.

Intended to bolster western stocks of AI technology and reduce “excessive dependencies” on single source supply chains, including from China, Pax Silica will provide chips and critical minerals to 26 participating signatory governments.
Amnesty International said demonstrations should not be forcibly or violently dispersed.

“Reports of arrests during the protests demand immediate scrutiny,” Amnesty’s director for the Philippines, Ritz Lee Santos III, said. “Authorities must explain the specific grounds for each arrest and any continued detention. Anyone detained solely for peacefully exercising their rights must be released immediately.”

articles.title: Chaos as crackdown on illegal mining in Guinea causes wave of regional displacement
articles.summary: Ban on illegal artisanal mining triggers mass exodus and diplomatic tensions with neighbouring Sahel states
body: In the border town of Kourémalé, split between Guinea and Mali, thousands of families have been trudging across the frontier over the past week after a sudden ban on illegal artisanal mining triggered a wave of displacement and a regional diplomatic dispute.

Some, like Seydou Traore, a miner in his 30s from Burkina Faso, made the 78-mile trek from Kourémalé to Ouezzindougou, farther inward. Last week, he gathered a small bundle of his belongings and fled Guinea after security forces ordered him and fellow miners to leave.
“We worked hard there, honestly,” he told Agence France-Presse (AFP). “Then one day everything changed. We were told to leave immediately, without even enough time to collect our tools or savings.”

He is among tens of thousands of people displaced across west Africa this month after Guinean authorities enforced the ban, citing the need to curb river pollution and deforestation, caused by large-scale illegal mining across the country, especially in the Siguiri area in the north-east.

In the days that followed, security agents raided mining hotspots, confiscating equipment and arresting 1,263 people. They also expelled thousands more: Mali says up to 160,000 miners fled into the Malian part of Kourémalé and as far as the capital, Bamako. At least six women have given birth in Mali since the displacement began in Guinea.

On 11 November, more than a week later, deadly violence broke out in the Balato community in Siguri, between security agents and miners erecting barricades. At least 10 people were killed and 13 others wounded, and three military vehicles were set alight.

The crackdown has triggered a regional diplomatic dispute: in a statement released on 12 November after a meeting in Ouagadougou, the Alliance of Sahel States said it recognised countries’ authority to enforce their laws, while voicing concern about the decree and expulsions.

Tiffany Wognaih, a senior analyst for the Francophone west and central Africa at geopolitical risk advisory JS Held, said illegal artisanal mining was widespread in the region, “especially in areas that aren’t necessarily continuously monitored by government presence”.
More than 300,000 people in Guinea eke out a living as illegal miners, according to data from the UN Environment Programme.

Many countries in the region lack comprehensive official numbers on gold export and processing. Conakry has remained defiant in the face of its neighbours’ displeasure. Mamady Doumbouya’s administration has grand ambitions to make Guinea a dominant mining force in the region and increase state revenues by tracking most of the value chain for resources such as gold.

The ban on illegal mining was announced a day after Guinea’s first gold refinery, the Nimba Gold Refinery, was officially launched with a declared annual processing capacity of 733 tonnes, far above the country’s annual gold output of 72 tonnes.

“If you’re opening a gold refinery, you need official supplies of gold to flow through the country’s channels,” Wognaih said. “And if a lot of it is being exported out of the country through illegal means and channels, then you don’t have enough processing in the country or showing up on official export figures.”

A year ago, the vast Simandou mine came on stream after nearly three decades of delay, to exploit one of the world’s biggest iron ore deposits. The $20bn project has rapidly ramped up shipments in the run-up to an annual target of 120m tonnes.

Meanwhile, concern is mounting within the Sahel states that the influx will exacerbate a humanitarian crisis that the military juntas are already struggling to contain amid insecurity and soaring living costs.
“These people are vulnerable,” a Malian security ministry official told AFP about the new arrivals. “We are looking at ways to prevent them from being approached by terrorist networks.”

articles.title: Tuesday briefing: Andy Burnham’s government wants to get young people into work. Will cutting their benefits help?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: Guaranteed jobs and expanded employment support sit alongside Alan Milburn’s proposals to cut benefits for some of Britain’s million young people not in education, work or training
body: Good morning. The former health secretary, Alan Milburn, will publish his long-awaited review into the one million young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) later today. The report will propose cutting welfare for some under-25s and spending billions on a new “deal” for young people. The government is at pains to tell you that its approach to welfare is nothing like that of the Tories’: Labour isn’t the party of “crude” benefit cuts, and it sees youth worklessness as a “moral” issue for which young people aren’t to blame.

It’s hard to recall a government report more heavily trailed than this one. It envisages a new relationship between young people and the state, and aims to get more young people into work and education while addressing the cost of young people becoming Neets. But will it work? For today’s First Edition, I spoke to the Guardian’s economics correspondent Richard Partington for a no-nonsense guide to all the things the government will say about this review, and how we should assess their arguments. First, here are the headlines.

UK | The Ministry of Justice has launched an investigation into whether Russell Brand has broken prison rules after the jailed comedian shared a message claiming he was not guilty of sexual offences just days after his conviction.

Israel | The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians, the Guardian can reveal.

EU | Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

UK news | Police chiefs say officers are “retreating from the streets” amid the worst financial crisis in decades, which has left nine forces seeking exceptional financial support (EFS) from the government.
Technology | Microsoft has identified the root causes of the global outage that crippled Outlook, Exchange and a host of other vital office software last week.

Remember when Keir Starmer’s government was forced to back-track last year after backbench Labour MPs voted against its controversial welfare reform bill, which proposed cutting personal independence payments (Pip)? Andy Burnham’s government is keen to avoid a repeat of that scenario, and Milburn has been assiduously trying to win over Labour MPs, as Pippa Crerar wrote yesterday. “The government is taking on an incredibly thorny issue, but they’re presenting this as a way to inject hope for the next generation,” Richard says. “They’re offsetting the negative stuff with a vast increase in employment support.”

Journalists will spend much of this week asking whether Milburn and Burnham have succeeded where Starmer failed. But the real test of their proposals lies far beyond SW1. Neets have been a concern for policymakers since the 1990s, and their number is now higher than ever. Among comparable European nations, only Romania had a higher Neet rate than Britain in 2025. The problem is also unevenly distributed: the likelihood of becoming Neet is (unsurprisingly) far higher in places like Blackpool than in the Cotswolds.

The report tries to address two problems. One is economic: more than a third of Neets do not claim benefits, but the cost of supporting those who do is high. Milburn estimates that £3.2bn of welfare spending on young people who are Neet could be avoided if they were in work. The other is more complex, and reflects a sense of generational despondency among young people, many of whom are “struggling to stay in sync with society at large”, as William Davies wrote in an interesting piece earlier this year (£).
What is Milburn’s review proposing?

• Big changes to welfare for young people: The report proposes the largest overhaul of the benefits system since the creation of universal credit in 2013. It suggests replacing Pip for under-25s and the health element of universal credit with a new “youth allowance”, which would be paid at the standard rate of UC.

• Guaranteed work: In exchange for losing access to their benefits, the government will “guarantee” eligible 18-to-24-year-olds a fully funded, six-month job. This builds on the Starmer government’s jobs guarantee, which was meant to be available to people who had been claiming UC for 18 months. The new proposals would extend eligibility for this to people who have been claiming UC for 12 months.

• More support for young people and employers: Instant (albeit digital) access to mental health support will be provided for young people who are Neet. Employers that hire people who have been Neet for six months will get a payment of £3,000, and the government is also expected to lower national insurance payments by businesses for employees aged between 21 and 24 for a five-year period, starting in retail and hospitality sectors.
What are some of the arguments in favour of these proposals?

Young people don’t want to be out of work. About 84% of young people who are Neet say they want to find a job, education or training. “Being out of work has a huge impact on your sense of wellbeing and mental health, and your finances,” Richard says. A 24-year-old who has never had a job will lose an estimated £300,000 in earnings over their lifetime, even after they enter the labour market. Milburn is proposing an “opportunity” guarantee, giving people support into education, training and work, and a “support” guarantee, allowing them to take this opportunity up. Expect more details on those later today.

Helping young people prepare for work is pointless if nobody wants to hire them. Milburn is expected to make a variation of this argument today. Young people now make up about 40% of the headline unemployment figures, partly because many employers aren’t willing to take a risk on them. But there’s also a risk that paying firms to employ people will benefit companies that would have hired them anyway, effectively handing public money to large corporations that really don’t need it.“Employers have a social responsibility,” Richard says. “But they often make a kneejerk argument for tax cuts and deregulation.”

If you don’t tackle this, your enemies will tackle it for you. The Department for Work and Pensions currently spends 25 times as much on benefits for young people than it does on employment support, something that many MPs believe is unsustainable, even if they find it hard to swallow cuts. “For Labour, there’s a danger that because welfare reform is difficult, it means it should never be touched,” Richard says. “You can imagine a different government taking a very different approach to this.”
What are some of the arguments against them?

Cutting benefits is unnecessary. While the review is being sold as an opportunity for young people, there’s no getting away from the fact that many young people will lose their benefits. About 184,000 young people aged 16 to 24 receive the universal credit health element, some of whom have complex needs that prohibit them from working. Benefits aren’t the cause of people becoming Neet, and if the government was solely interested in creating opportunities for young people, it could do so without cutting welfare. As more people enter the labour market, the number of people on benefits will reduce.

Work doesn’t pay. Governments often treat the labour market as a solution to the rising welfare bill while ignoring the reality of modern work. In-work poverty has been rising over the last decade and many benefit claimants have been forced into low-paid, part-time jobs on zero-hours contracts. As Richard noted earlier this week, countless studies connect badly paid work to poor mental wellbeing. In other words, it’s not enough to funnel young people into jobs. The pay, conditions and quality of those jobs also matter.

Neets are symptomatic of bigger problems. The rate of Neets is higher in disadvantaged and deindustrialised areas where there are fewer jobs. “If there aren’t jobs to go to, what chance of success do you have?” Richard says. In that sense, the proposed changes risk hitting the most disadvantaged the hardest. For the Milburn report’s proposals to work, Richard believes they will need to form part of a wider strategy to create prosperity in places outside the UK’s major cities. Otherwise, the government will simply be managing the consequences of an economic crisis, rather than addressing its cause.

Floods and bombings: Deadly winter approaches in Gaza

Deadly floods in Gaza have created a dire humanitarian crisis, as the governments of Australia, Canada, the UK and Italy call on Israel to allow the safe passage of critical aid to civilians before winter sets in. Tens of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza have been left in waterlogged and damaged tents, with sanitation infrastructure also destroyed by storms. Supplies including food, medicine and water and 150,000 tents are being held by Israel at the border, while the UN warns of the spread of diseases. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s chief Middle East correspondent, Emma Graham-Harrison.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

When Georgina Lawton returned to England after a four and a half year stint away in Lisbon, it was depressing at first. She returned in winter, to higher prices and faster pace of life, and a new diagnosis made everything feel that little bit harder. That’s until she picked up a new hobby: ice-skating.

Grabbing some skates and heading to the rink twice a week vastly improved the way she experienced life. Suddenly, life felt full of progress and social connection – and the structure helped with a feeling of aimlessness. She went and bought her first pair of proper skates, and found herself with a new friendship group, aged anywhere from 15-60.
“Friends who had always said I was “all or nothing” joked that I would drop my new hobby when things got tough, but I persisted,” says Lawton.
