articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Crimea bridge attacked again after Russia strikes major Kyiv bridges
articles.summary: Ukraine again hits symbolic bridge linking occupied Crimea to Russia; Kyiv’s heating and water disrupted as North and South bridges struck. What we know on day 1,728
body: Ukraine struck a symbolic bridge that links the annexed Crimean peninsula to Russia for the second day in a row, after Moscow launched strikes on Kyiv’s bridges. Crimea’s Moscow-installed governor Sergey Aksyonov said on Tuesday that Ukrainian forces had struck the bridge and traffic had been suspended. On Monday, a Ukrainian drone crashed into one of the Kerch bridge’s arches. Ukraine says the bridge is a legitimate target for its armed forces, and has made at least two previous attempts to blow it up. Aksyonov also said on Tuesday that two people were ⁠killed ⁠in ​a Ukrainian drone attack ⁠on Crimea.

Russian strikes hit two major bridges in Kyiv late on Monday, part of an overnight attack that damaged critical infrastructure and disrupted heating and water in parts of the Ukrainian capital, its mayor said. The North and South bridges were hit, Vitali Klitschko said, citing preliminary information, in a post on Telegram just before midnight local time (2200 GMT), shortly after the Ukrainian air force warned of incoming missiles. He later said critical infrastructure systems were damaged and that heating and water supplies in some districts were affected. Air defence units were in operation in the city, he said, while witnesses ‌reported a series of loud explosions.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy had earlier warned of an attack by Russia in the coming days. “Tonight, overnight and throughout tomorrow, please pay attention to missile danger alerts,” the Ukrainian president said in his nightly video address on Monday. “And they there, in Russia, must know that for every one of their evils there will be our just response.”

Russia is receiving “dozens of missiles per month” from North Korea, Zelenskyy has said, citing a report from Ukraine’s HUR main intelligence directorate. “This is ​extremely dangerous and not ​only for Ukraine,” the president said. “By using ​its ballistic missiles in this war, North Korea is making ​its weapons more ‌effective. This creates ​additional challenges for the ​entire region around Korea.” Zelenskyy called on European allies to send more weapons to respond “on equal terms” to the threat.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine had held new online ⁠talks with US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, as well as European representatives, on the prospects of ⁠ending the war with Russia. The talks came less than a week after US, Ukrainian and Russian officials held their first three-way ⁠talks in nine months in Abu Dhabi. “Diplomatic processes are actively underway and we hope ​that these efforts will not be ‌in vain,” Zelenskyy said on Monday. “Our ‌team is working in the most constructive manner possible.”

Zelenskyy said European representatives – including ‌from France, the UK, Germany, Italy and Poland – took part in full and would be represented in the same way in future meetings with Russian negotiators. The discussion was “not easy”, the Ukrainian president said, without elaborating. But he said all had agreed to meet at talks in Berlin with the “coalition of the willing” countries supporting ‌Ukraine. In Moscow, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Russia had not yet agreed to the participation of European representatives in the next round ​of Ukraine peace talks, contradicting comments by US negotiators after talks in Moscow that the Europeans would be at the next negotiations.

The International Monetary Fund said it made important ⁠progress ⁠in discussions with ​Ukrainian authorities on a staff-level agreement ⁠that would free up $1.6bn in funds ⁠for Kyiv, once financing assurances ​had been ‌secured. It said IMF staff ‌and Ukraine were engaging with international partners to ​secure the financing assurances needed due to the expected longer duration ⁠of the war, it said.

articles.title: Rio Tinto agrees to pay US$250m to begin repairing ‘devastation’ left by Panguna mine
articles.summary: Community leader says fund gives chance to find solutions to ‘huge problems we have been living with since the days of the mine’s operation’
body: Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto has agreed to pay a quarter-of-a-billion dollars to begin the clean-up of the toxic Panguna mine site it abandoned more than three decades ago.

Panguna, once one of the world’s most profitable gold and copper mines, was shuttered in 1989 after violent protests over environmental damage and the inequitable division of the mine’s profits sparked a decade-long civil war on the Papua New Guinean island of Bougainville.
But the sprawling mine pit, once a mountain, remains a scar in the middle of the island, with vast pillars of rubble at risk of collapse, and polluted rivers running bright blue with toxins.
Related: Bougainville fought a war to shut down Panguna mine. Now it wants to reopen it

Rio Tinto was forced from the island and has never returned, but in recent years has been part of a detailed consultation process with landowners and government. It has now agreed to voluntarily contribute US$250m (A$370m) towards the remediation of the mine site.

Theonila Roka Matbob, a former cabinet minister in Bougainville’s autonomous government and Panguna community leader, said the fund was a vital contribution towards repairing the “devastation left by the Panguna mine”.

“We have a lot of work still ahead of us, but the establishment of this fund gives us the chance to find solutions to the huge problems we have been living with since the days of the mine’s operation.

“No amount of money will restore the damage caused to the environment in Panguna, but this sets a foundation for us to invest in addressing the environmental issues and invest in our children’s futures as well.”

Roka Matbob said the most fundamental remediation was to improve “accessibility” for the people living around Panguna – “accessibility to clean drinking water that is safe and secure … and infrastructure, in bridges that makes people’s access to trade, to school, to health[care], much easier. This is one critical area that immediately needs attention.”

The president of Bougainville, Ishmael Toroama, seeking to become the world’s newest head of state at the forefront of a long-running independence movement on the island, said the money would make a “meaningful difference” to villages and communities that had suffered from the impacts of the mine’s pollution.

“This work will deliver benefits not only for people today, but for future generations. Continued engagement with our communities will be essential to ensuring the work responds to local priorities and delivers lasting outcomes.”

The Rio commitment has emerged from the Panguna Mine Legacy Impact Assessment consultation process, which was initiated in response to a human rights complaint brought by the Australian-based Human Rights Law Centre, with Roka Matbob as the lead complainant.
Keren Adams, the HRLC’s legal director, said establishing the fund had taken years of work.
Related: ‘No one will stop our people’: Bougainville president defiant in push for independence
“It is a testament to the courage and persistence of community leaders, and the willingness of all parties to engage in difficult but constructive dialogue,” she said.
“The significant funding contributed by Rio Tinto creates a real opportunity to now address an environmental disaster that has remained unresolved for decades.”

Mark Davies, Rio Tinto’s chief safety and technical officer, said the establishment of the fund was an “important milestone … intended to support the transition from the assessment to practical remedy implementation”.
“Community engagement is an important next step to identify priorities and we remain committed to working with communities to shape the activities supported by the fund.”
The quarter-of-a-billion dollars will not be sufficient to entirely remediate the mine site, but it is being seen as a major step towards rehabilitation.
The funding commitment for Panguna comes at an acutely sensitive time for the restive Bougainville island.

The mine has become inextricably linked with the Bougainville’s political future: restarting operations at Panguna – believed to still hold at least $60bn in unrealised reserves – is seen by many, including the president, as the fundamental financial basis for the island’s independent future. Indian miner Lloyds has been granted a 25-year large-scale mining lease, but any future mining is years from starting.
Bougainville, a group of islands off Papua New Guinea to the north of Australia, has been variously controlled by Britain, Germany, Japan, Australia and PNG.
It declared independence in 1975 as the Republic of North Solomons, but was absorbed into the newly independent PNG weeks later.
Its close ethnic ties and proximity to the Solomons archipelago means it has always sat uneasily with Port Moresby’s rule.
That discontent came to a violent head in 1988 after a long-running dispute over the lucrative Panguna copper and gold mine.
The mine, carved from a mountain in central Bougainville, was critically important to PNG, at one point generating more than 45% of the country's national export revenue.

Multinational Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly US$2bn from the mine over 17 years of operation. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands had been destroyed by it.
Under the leadership of a former mine worker, Francis Ona, disaffected Bougainvilleans ran a sabotage campaign which forced the mine’s closure in 1989.

The PNG Government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war that ran for a decade, and saw as many as 20,000 people die.
PNG later hired international mercenaries to end the conflict (the notorious Sandline affair), before a peace agreement was signed in 2001.
In a 2019 referendum, 97.7% of Bougainvilleans voted in favour of independence. Many argue that reopening Panguna mine will be key to the island’s economic future as an independent nation.

Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly $2bn from Panguna over 17 years of operation from 1972. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands were destroyed by it.

Disaffected landowners ran a sabotage campaign that forced Panguna’s closure in 1989. The PNG government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war – known as “the crisis” – that ran for a decade. Between 15,000 and 20,000 people were killed, roughly 10% of the island’s population.
Related: ‘Cut the umbilical cord’: Bougainville’s bid to break away from Papua New Guinea faces reckoning

A recent environmental impact assessment found the abandoned mine remains an acute threat to people’s lives, including from landslides, levee collapses and floods. Untouched, the river delta will stay polluted for a century.

The future of Bougainville’s independence campaign is now before the PNG parliament, which will decide whether or not to recognise a UN-backed independence referendum held on the island in 2019, in which 97.7% of voters were in favour of Bougainville seceding and becoming an independent country.
The PNG parliament, which heard lengthy and impassioned debate over Bougainville last month, appears almost certain to vote against recognising the referendum result.

But Toroama, who has staked his presidency on achieving political independence, has said, regardless of the parliament’s decision, Bougainville will enter a period of “self-government” from September next year, before seceding, breaking away from PNG as a fully fledged independent nation, by 2030.

articles.title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
articles.summary: Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’
body: Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.

In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.

Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.

In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.
Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.

The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.
The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.
Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.

The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”

Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”

Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.

Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, said on Monday the move had no “future or humanity”. “I don’t see any future or humanity in that. It’s not the solution,” Sanchez, an outspoken defender of immigration in a Europe that has tilted to the right in recent years, told Telecinco television.

The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”

Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.
“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.
Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.

Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia strategy challenged by anti-Houthi forces in Yemen
articles.summary: Accusations of incompetence follow retreat of Riyadh-backed forces in effort to relieve siege of Taiz and protect Aden
body: Saudi Arabia has been accused by anti-Houthi forces over its military strategy after its Yemeni allies withdrew troops from the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and pulled back forces from parts of Marib in the central part of the country.

The Saudi-backed government explained the repositioning by saying the strategic priority was to break the attritional siege on Taiz, Yemen’s third city, and to protect Aden, the southern port city in which the Saudi-backed and UN-recognised government is now based.

Many blame the Houthi advance on the absence of a consolidated military command and control among the disparate forces backing the Aden-based government. Saudi Arabia responded to the setback by sidelining the commander of its Yemen coalition, Lt Gen Fahd bin Abdulaziz al-Salman, and replacing him with the chief of staff, Gen Fayyad bin Hamed bin Ruqad al-Ruwaili.

The Houthis’ steady advance towards the areas surrounding Bab al-Mandab, the narrow strait linking the Red Sea with the Indian Ocean on Yemen’s west coast, culminated on Sunday with a formal withdrawal of Yemen government forces, including some in the Southern Giants Brigades that had always been reluctant to defend territory outside the old southern Yemen. In 1990 Yemen had been divided in two, and many in the south want to return to a separated state.
The Saudi-backed government launched a fresh military campaign 42 days ago to drive the Houthis from Yemen but so far it has backfired.
The forces redeployed on Sunday have moved along the coast to al-Suqyah, 95 miles west of Aden, and inside the old Southern Yemen.
The retreat seems to be acknowledgment of Houthi resilience and is all the more remarkable given the Saudi air superiority. More than 300,000 Yemeni civilians have been displaced.

Amr al-Bidh, special representative of the exiled Southern Transitional Council (STC) leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, a separatist anti-Houthi force that is opposed by Saudi Arabia, accused the Saudis of incompetence – and in effect warned Riyadh that unless it became more open to a southern state it would lack the cohesive forces required to prevent the Houthis becoming a permanent security threat.
Related: Yemen’s president sacks ministers and officers in attempt to turn tide of war

He said: “When there is no strategy and no plan, it is inevitable the Houthis would take advantage. The STC will defend the south to the last man but we are fighting with one hand behind our backs since January after Saudi Arabia attacks on the STC.

“The STC forces retain a credible capability on the ground. But we need practical and political support from the region to counter the Houthis and create the basis for a negotiated settlement, one in which the pathway towards southern independence is fully recognised. We cannot continue like this or else the Houthis will keep expanding.”

The breadth of support for the STC, backed by the United Arab Emirates, however, remains disputed. The movement suffered a near fatal setback in January and since then some of the Giants Brigades have switched to backing Riyadh.

Saudi Arabia continues in effect to keep as many as 10 STC leaders hostage in Riyadh, and has refused to let al-Zubaidi to return from exile in Abu Dhabi. Al-Bidh argued the priority should be defensive, avoiding counteroffensives that backfire, improving command and control, and widening the coalition.

Al-Bidh said reconciliation would require Riyadh to acknowledge the political declaration al-Zubaidi made about a timetable for a southern state in January, and that al-Zubaidi’s return would boost morale and help unify chaotic southern military factions.

He said a recent Yemeni government cabinet reshuffle, including a new information minister, was designed primarily to try draw southerners into fighting the Houthis and not to change policy toward the south.

He also urged the UK to use its diplomacy to bring in other actors rather than simply backing Riyadh. A group of southern Yemenis have written to the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, seeking a review of UK policy. “We recognise that the longstanding advice from your office is to continue following the Saudi line while calling for unity among the anti-Houthi forces,” the letter said. “But you must surely recognise that every time Britain calls for ‘the unity and territorial integrity of Yemen’, it is asking the southern people and their armed forces to fight for a political outcome in which they do not believe”.

The former US special envoy to Yemen Tim Lenderking said the US administration was treating Yemen like a sideshow adding “world powers do not understand the gravity of what it is at stake here”. He warned “the problem is only going to get bigger through apathy and lack of attention”.
• This article was amended on 16 November 2026. An early version misquoted Amr al-Bidh as saying it is inevitable “the Saudis” would take advantage in Yemen. This was corrected to “the Houthis”.

articles.title: Xi, Trump and Putin to discuss ‘world peace’ at trilateral, says China
articles.summary: Beijing stops short of confirming specific agenda, but Trump says denuclearisation, Iran war, trade and Ukraine will be among topics
body: The meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen this week will cover topics of “groundbreaking significance” including “safeguarding world peace”, the Chinese foreign ministry has said.

The confirmation of Thursday’s trilateral talks, the first of their kind, will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and cement Xi’s status as a global power broker as he presides over events in the glittering southern tech hub of Shenzhen.

At the White House, Trump told reporters he would be speaking to his Chinese and Russian counterparts about denuclearisation, the war in Iran, economics, trade and “my favourite subject, Ukraine”. US officials had earlier indicated that Trump would not discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine during the trip.

Trump also said he may meet North Korea’s Kim Jong-un in what would be their first meeting of his second term. “We may meet with Kim Jong-un also,” Trump said. “So that will be good … we have a chance to accomplish a lot.”
Asked whether Kim would be there, Trump said that he “may come”. “I don’t know,” he said. “That’s up to president Xi.”
Many, including the UN secretary general, António Guterres, had hoped the trilateral talks would be used to discuss reductions in nuclear arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers.

In a call this week, China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation”, the US state department said.
China was the last of the three powers to confirm the trilateral meeting was happening, and its statement stopped short of confirming specific agenda items.

“[The leaders] will exchange views in-depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” said its foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning. “Stronger communication among China, Russia and the United States, along ​with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries.”
The Kremlin said: “The significance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate.”

Separately, the Kremlin ‌spokesperson Dmitry Peskov reportedly said on Monday that Putin would meet Kim, too, ​were he to be invited. “Of course, if ‌he is at the APEC ​summit,” Interfax quoted Peskov as saying. Peskov made ⁠his comments as ​Putin met ​a ​delegation in ​the Kremlin ‌from North ​Korea’s ​ruling Workers party.

Guterres said that if the three leaders “really commit themselves to a meaningful denuclearisation, it will be a great achievement for the world”. However, many analysts have warned to temper expectations of a major breakthrough.

Xi will “bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter”, wrote Brookings’ Ryan Hass in one such take. However, “symbolism may prove more enduring than the substance of this meeting”.
The three leaders would be approaching the talks with very different priorities, Xiaoyu Pu from the University of Nevada told the Guardian.
Related: Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up?

China has rebuffed previous attempts to become embroiled in nuclear arms talks with ​Russia and the US, which ‌have the larger stockpiles. Trump, though, has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation, as well as the US-Israeli war in Iran. China, a top economic partner of Tehran, has sought to mediate in the conflict and says avoiding a return to hostilities is a “top priority”.

Trump’s remarks that he wanted to discuss Ukraine could stoke fears voiced by the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, that the trilateral talks could turn into a “Yalta 2, 3, 4 with a redistribution of influence”. Zelenskyy was referring to the 1945 pact between the US, UK and Soviet Union that created spheres of influence in Europe after the second world war.

“Ukraine-Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers a month, so we’ll be talking about that,” Trump said. He also deflected criticism of Putin in his remarks, saying the Kremlin leader could be “a lot tougher” in Ukraine and that he was already “backing down”.

US officials had said Trump was not expected to raise the issue, and the German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, said Xi showed “irritation” in a recent meeting when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up.
For Xi, much of the political benefit will be simply in “the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table”, Peter Alexander, the Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors, told CNBC.

The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the Trump administration had pushed back against Beijing’s demands that the summit be tightly scripted, with prepared statements and not much room for discussion.

Sari Arho Havrén, of the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, wrote on X: “China dislikes surprises and wants to ensure neither Trump nor Putin steals the limelight from the host. Moreover, Xi doesn’t want to be dragged into a discussion about Ukraine or anything else he is not prepared for.”

articles.title: Sreelata Tottingham obituary
articles.summary: Other lives: Human rights activist who helped increase Amnesty International’s influence in the Asia-Pacific region
body: My friend Sreelata Tottingham, who has died aged 73, spent more than a decade working with the human-rights organisation Amnesty International in the late 1970s and 80s. As regional officer for Asia-Pacific, she was tasked with developing Amnesty’s presence throughout Asia at a pivotal time for the organisation, making full use of her fluent English, Hindi and Bengali. She succeeded brilliantly, and Amnesty’s presence and influence spread throughout the region, and with it a growing concern for human rights. Her colleagues at the time described her as an inspirational figure.

After leaving Amnesty she focused her efforts on improving lives in poorer parts of London, working for the North Peckham Task Force, a government inner-city initiative, as well as for Camden and Lambeth borough councils, and for the Refugee Council, a charitable organisation that supports refugees and asylum seekers.

Sreelata was born in New Delhi, the daughter of Eric Da Costa, who introduced opinion polling to India for Gallup, and his wife, Leila. Brought up in Khetri House, a gift to her parents from the Raja of Khetri, Sreelata was surrounded by India’s political, diplomatic and economic elite.

From that background came her concern for others and a lively, inquiring personality and mind. After leaving the Convent of Jesus and Mary, she gained an economics degree at the University of Delhi, and a master’s at the Delhi School of Economics, and began her working life at the Gallup Institute in New Delhi. She joined Amnesty International after moving to London in 1979.
In 1985 she married Richard Tottingham, and they had two daughters, Leila and Nadia.

Towards the end of her life, Sreelata retrained as a psychotherapist, providing counselling to many through Southwark Carers and Cruse Bereavement and also in private practice, focusing on those bereaved. She was a parishioner at St Mary’s, Clapham, and attended the Shambala Buddhist Centre. She saw no contradiction in this and contributed to and benefited from both faiths. She was also a caring and much-loved grandmother, revelling in spoiling the next generation. Across all her connections she is remembered as a thoughtful and resilient woman, with a deep interest in people and supporting those she met.
Sreelata is survived by Richard, Leila and Nadia, her granddaughters, Iris and Annika, and her brother, Francis.

articles.title: ‘Visceral response’: flag campaigns inspire anti-racism organising across England
articles.summary: Exclusive: Study shows people taking action against far-right intimidation such as 75-year-old taking to his bike at 2am to remove flags
body: Flag campaigns and far-right intimidation have sparked a wave of grassroots anti-racism organising across England in the past 12 months, according to research.

The Institute of Race Relations (IRR) says the widespread displays of St George’s cross and union jack flags have been accompanied by racist abuse and violence, with flags deliberately placed outside schools, mosques and care homes.
The report also warns that flag campaigns may be serving as recruitment grounds for far-right vigilantism, pointing to links between local groups and more militant anti-migrant networks.

But the report notes that the campaigns have also prompted ordinary residents to take action, from Quakers devising homemade tools to remove flags in Oxford to community groups documenting racist incidents in south-west London and establishing solidarity hubs in Nottingham.

Sophia Siddiqui, the report’s author, said she had been struck by the anger and frustration among people who felt compelled to act. “One person I spoke to, a 75-year-old man who has never been an activist before, seeing what was happening around him really provoked a visceral response, where he just felt like he had to get on his bike at 2am and start taking down flags.”

Siddiqui said the campaigns had “backfired” in some communities. “Whenever flags had gone up, it had been met with community resistance, which had had the opposite effect of actually bringing people together.”
Last year, St George’s cross and union jack flags appeared across England in campaigns organisers described as patriotic, but which critics linked to racist intimidation and harassment.

Ryan Bridge, a co-founder of one of the initiatives, Raise the Colours, was charged earlier this year with 14 offences, including racially aggravated harassment and assault. Bridge pleaded not guilty to all charges earlier this month.
The report, Anti-fascism from below: resistance to far-right flag campaigns, draws on interviews with community organisers in Oxford, Birmingham, London, Nottingham and Worcestershire.

Siddiqui said flag campaigns had been accompanied by racist abuse against schoolchildren, Islamophobic harassment and racist graffiti, while flags deliberately placed outside schools, care homes and places of worship in multicultural areas had created “an atmosphere of intimidation”.
Related: ‘Not a culture war’: the council that won its case over England flags on lampposts

In Oxford, members of the Quaker community became so concerned about the displays that they devised their own method of removing them. George, a spokesperson for Oxford Quakers who didn’t wish to give his real name, said residents feared the flags were giving a false impression of a city with a long history of welcoming refugees and asylum seekers.
“What we really disliked was the colonising of our public space by people with opposing views to give the impression that Oxford was a xenophobic place, which it definitively is not,” he said.

With the council initially removing only flags considered hazardous, and council workers reportedly facing abuse and intimidation for attempting to take the flags down, the Quakers fashioned a tool using a blade attached to an 8-metre wooden pole to cut down flags.
“We just thought there must be another clever way that will be discreet and non-confrontational. That’s the Quaker way,” George said.

In south-west London, Saqib Deshmukh, co-founder of Merton Against Racism, began documenting flag displays after spotting them on his regular running route in Colliers Wood. “I got on my bike to cycle around, and lo and behold, there were flags everywhere,” he said.
He set up a spreadsheet tracking flags and painted crosses across the borough, cross-referencing incidents with reports to the council. His group recorded nearly 50 incidents.
Deshmukh also described reports of racist abuse directed at Black and Asian residents in streets where flags had appeared, including near schools, nurseries and a care home employing migrant workers.
“This wasn’t done willy-nilly. This was very carefully orchestrated and thought through,” he said.
Despite residents lobbying councillors, contacting their MP and raising concerns at council meetings, Deshmukh said many flags remained until deteriorating weather brought them down.

In Nottingham, organisers have taken a different approach, establishing a solidarity centre in Hyson Green that offers food, legal advice, art workshops and a space for people from different backgrounds to meet.
Jagdish Patel, who is involved in the initiative, said the aim was to tackle the economic insecurity and isolation that far-right groups exploit.
“We feed people, and by feeding people, people from all different backgrounds come together,” he said.

Elsewhere last year, counter-protesters vastly outnumbered the Worcester Patriots at a demonstration in Worcester, while Birmingham residents launched a citywide solidarity poster campaign. In Oxford, community pressure helped secure an injunction against unauthorised flags on lamp-posts, with Birmingham pursuing similar action.

But challenging far-right activity has carried risks. Patel described cases of white women being harassed for expressing sympathy towards asylum seekers, while the report documents activists facing threats, intimidation and online doxxing.
The IRR warns that flag campaigns may have provided a recruitment route into more militant far-right vigilantism.
Siddiqui pointed to the emergence of Patriotic Platform, which mobilised masked men at the ports of Kent and Portsmouth in September.
She said flagging campaigns, in seeking to impose their values on neighbourhoods and punish those who disagreed, “already had some of the hallmarks of vigilantism”.
Yet Siddiqui said the research had ultimately left her hopeful about the capacity of ordinary people to challenge the far right.

“What really stood out to me was the importance of building connections locally. It’s speaking to people, engaging with people, having those difficult conversations, and building those links at a local level,” she said.

articles.title: Ukraine hits Kerch bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea
articles.summary: Traffic temporarily restricted on key connection after bridge targeted during overnight drone barrage by Ukraine
body: Ukraine has hit the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia, in a symbolic blow that temporarily paralysed road traffic and left thousands of drivers stranded.

A Ukrainian kamikaze drone crashed into one of the bridge’s arches at 5.38am local time, local channels reported. Earlier drones could be heard buzzing above the structure, as Russian air defence units opened fire.
The extent of the damage was unclear. One report said the arch was listing at a 15-degree angle and “looked tired”.
The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed the “enemy” had launched an attack. “As a result, traffic will be restricted, likely until the afternoon,” he wrote on Telegram.
Related: Ukraine war briefing: Energy attacks made possible by continuing Starshield restrictions, says Zelenskyy
Russian officials said the crossing would remain closed while experts assessed its condition. About 2,000 vehicles were reportedly stuck in traffic jams on both sides.
In a call with reporters, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, downplayed the incident. He said: “Minor damage is being assessed. ⁠Traffic across the bridge continues.”
Ukraine says the bridge is a legitimate target for its armed forces, and has made at least two previous attempts to blow it up.

In 2022 a truck laden with explosives damaged part of the road section. A second strike using a “sea baby” drone took place the following year. Russia has subsequently strengthened air defences and installed metal barges and boom barriers.

Overnight Ukraine launched 1,336 drones, in what the Kremlin says was one of the biggest attacks so far this year. About 600 were intercepted at night on their approach to Moscow, claimed the capital’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, and more than 150 more throughout Monday.

The barrage took place days before a summit in Shenzhen between China’s president, Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin. US officials say the talks will not focus on the war in Ukraine, where Russia’s military offensive has largely stalled.

Ukraine says its retaliatory strikes are justified retribution for Russia’s own missile and drone barrages of its cities and energy grid – attacks that have killed hundreds of civilians and regularly knock out power and heating for millions. In recent weeks Russia has repeatedly hit two critical bridges in Kyiv over the Dnipro river.

Diplomatic efforts on ending the almost five-year war have so far gone nowhere. After a fresh round of talks in Abu Dhabi last week, Putin reiterated his hardline territorial demands and said any deployment of foreign troops would be seen in Moscow as a “continuation of war”.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Friday the Trump administration had proposed that Kyiv gives Russia the eastern Donbas region – including towns and villages Russia does not control – in exchange for Nato membership or Nato-like guarantees.

Zelenskyy ruled out handing over territory. The details of possible US security guarantees were vague and did not feature American troops on the ground, he said, citing conversations with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and the real-estate developer Steve Witkoff. The emissaries last week saw Putin in Moscow.

articles.title: Revealed: Israel uploaded millions of photos to Amazon’s facial recognition platform to track Palestinians
articles.summary: Upload came as the Israeli military was increasing its reliance on Amazon’s cloud platform to meet the technological demands of its bombardment of Gaza
body: The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians, the Guardian can reveal.
Leaked documents show the expansive catalogue of images was moved into Amazon’s cloud in the early months of Israel’s devastating aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza.
The images were uploaded by a department of the Israeli military that holds a vast collection of photos covering the Palestinian populations in Gaza and the West Bank.
The department informed Amazon of the decision to upload the images in early 2024 so it could use Rekognition, the company’s AI-powered image analysis platform for a facial recognition project.

The documents obtained by the Guardian form part of an investigation into the Israeli military’s reliance on the technology and infrastructure of Amazon’s cloud computing business to monitor Palestinians.

According to the files and interviews with military sources, Israel has in recent years migrated huge volumes of data – including sensitive intelligence material and information about Palestinians living under occupation – into Amazon’s datacentres.
The large set of images was moved into an Amazon datacentre near Tel Aviv by a department commonly known as Rolling Stone, which sits within a military software unit.
The department takes its name from a system widely used by the Israeli military that serves as a central repository of information about Palestinians living in Gaza and the West Bank.

At the time, the department was exploring using facial recognition technologies to analyse the extensive catalogues of images of Palestinians it holds, several sources with knowledge of its work said.

After Israel’s ground invasion of Gaza in October 2023, its military routinely collected images of Palestinians as they passed through checkpoints, often after they had been forcibly displaced by the bombing campaign.
It’s not clear whether the 3.5m images uploaded to Amazon’s Rekognition were captured at these checkpoints, which effectively served as pop-up surveillance posts.
However, a military source familiar with facial recognition efforts at the checkpoints said Amazon’s cloud infrastructure was used due to the “very large scale” of images collected at the sites.

Israel has long used facial recognition technology, particularly in its occupation of the West Bank. Face scanning is routine at checkpoints, while Israeli soldiers use custom-built smartphone apps to collect images of people living in the Palestinian territory.

In the early stages of its campaign in Gaza, Israel used Rekognition to identify hostages captured by militants in the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023. The military also deployed facial recognition technology to identify people it suspected were militants.

The New York Times has previously reported how the military experimented with commercially available technology in Gaza to detect faces in crowds and in drone footage, at times wrongly flagging civilians as militants.

The new documents reveal the Israeli military’s use of Amazon technology, both for experiments with facial recognition and for a more far-reaching project to move its data on to the servers of the computing arm of the conglomerate founded by billionaire Jeff Bezos.

They also shed light on what the Israeli military is moving into the cloud and how it uses Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure to support the collection and processing of Palestinians’ personal data, typically gathered indiscriminately, through intrusive means and without their consent.

The files suggest the ties between AWS and the Israeli military deepened during a period in which Israel has been accused of committing grave crimes in Gaza, including genocide – a charge denied by Israel, but supported by a UN commission of inquiry, Israeli human rights groups and genocide experts.

A spokesperson for AWS said it had no “visibility” into workloads held by its customers in its cloud. They added: “We respect the privacy of our customers, and we do not discuss our relationship without their consent.”
In early 2024, a small group of Israeli soldiers worked from AWS’s offices in Tel Aviv, located on the 28th floor of one of Israel’s tallest skyscrapers.
The soldiers were exploring ways to use the company’s cloud infrastructure to more effectively operate a facial recognition programme underway in Gaza, several military sources said.

It’s not clear whether their work was made operational or if it related to the 3.5m images uploaded to Rekognition. The presence of the group at AWS’s offices, however, underscores the close relationship between the Israeli military and the cloud provider.

An AWS spokesperson said its customers “regularly visit our offices for briefings and meetings”. They added: “Any suggestion that these visits are anything other than routine customer engagement is wrong and unsubstantiated.”

The foundation of Israel’s relationship with Amazon is a sweeping 2021 contract known as Project Nimbus. Under the multibillion dollar deal, AWS and Google provide cloud services to a wide range of government and military clients.

The Guardian revealed last year that the Nimbus contract contains unusual terms that prohibit the US companies from restricting or suspending Israeli government and military use of their cloud services, even if Israel breaches their terms of service.

This would prevent the kind of unilateral action taken by Microsoft last year when it disabled the Israeli military’s access to technology used to operate a mass surveillance system uncovered by the Guardian and +972 Magazine.

As part of the Nimbus deal, AWS opened new datacentres in Israel in early 2023, allowing the Israeli government and military clients to migrate data from their own servers, according to documents. A large proportion of data was also moved from AWS datacentres in Ireland.

A central component of the Nimbus contract, files show, was an obligation on AWS to provide the Israeli military with access to a segregated area within its Tel Aviv datacentres, fortified with enhanced digital and physical security measures.

This isolated area within the AWS cloud – used to store sensitive material relating to military operations and intelligence collection – was described by the company and its client as a “walled garden”.

The Israeli military’s reliance on AWS reflects its embrace in recent years of leading US tech companies to meet the technological demands of war with rapidly scalable storage, computing power and AI-driven services.

The role of AI in Israel’s offensive in Gaza has come under fresh scrutiny particularly after the release of NAZA, a Guardian-produced documentary about the remote surveillance and killing of Palestinian civilians.

The Rolling Stone department is among AWS’s most significant Israeli military clients, documents suggest. Its use of Rekognition in early 2024 to analyse 3.5m images came after it had expanded its use of AWS products and services to store and analyse its data.

Files show the department migrated significant volumes of the data it holds into the so-called “walled garden” in AWS’s cloud throughout 2023. A military source involved in this effort said it had planned to move all of its databases from the military servers into AWS’s cloud.
The source, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said: “The plan [at Rolling Stone] was to migrate pictures, videos, all the confidential intelligence information – everything.”
A spokesperson for the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said it “does not intend to comment on engagements or services related to operational needs”.
The Rolling Stone department oversees several expansive databases that collate data on Palestinians, including the system from which the branch takes its name.

Used by the military for decades, the Rolling Stone system is constantly updated and includes data such as basic personal and family details, property holdings, and information on checkpoint crossings, work permits, and criminal activity.

A soldier who provided testimony to Breaking the Silence, an Israeli NGO, in 2016 described Rolling Stone as “a computerised system where all the information relevant to the control of the Palestinian civilian population is centralised”.

As a result of Israel’s control of the population registries covering Gaza and the West Bank, the Rolling Stone department has amassed millions of Palestinians’ photographs taken for the identity cards issued to every resident when they turn 16 years old.

Sources familiar with its work said the images were routinely used for facial recognition programmes. These include Blue Wolf, a smartphone app Israeli soldiers use in the West Bank to scan Palestinians’ faces and access information about them, including whether they’ve been flagged as suspects for arrest.

In Gaza, at temporary Israeli checkpoints established after the ground invasion, cameras trained on Palestinian people were used to capture their images as they approached the sites. Facial recognition was then used to match people to images held in Rolling Stone’s systems, sources said.

The checkpoints became notorious in Gaza as places where people were pulled aside and detained. Many were taken into Israeli custody and held incommunicado, amounting to enforced disappearances, according to several UN bodies and rights groups.

Documents suggest AWS’s cloud technology was used at times during 2024 to support the work of the checkpoints. Military insiders said the checkpoints were referred to by Israeli soldiers as Nakaz – a Hebrew word for drainage.

Harry Davies is one of the Guardian producers on NAZA, which Yuval Abraham co-directed. NAZA is now in cinemas worldwide and will screen for free on the Guardian’s website from early December. Sign up here to be the first to watch it

articles.title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
articles.summary: Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human
body: The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.
Related: ‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeys

The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. Some animal rights activists have compared authorities’ baboon management to apartheid.
During Friday’s relocation, outraged protesters tried to stop vehicles taking the baboons away. One person sprayed a fire extinguisher, according to the Daily Maverick, a local news outlet.

After the confrontation, the local Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals branch urged those opposed to the baboons’ capture not to try to stop the vehicles. “Capture and transport are already stressful for the baboons,” it said in a statement. “Delaying their arrival prolongs their time in crates and risks adding to that stress – this is not fair on the baboons.”
It said it remained opposed to the baboon’s relocation, adding: “Our presence did not imply support … our inspectors are present because the animals need someone looking out for them.”

On Sunday, dozens of people sat outside the wildlife centre in a silent protest, some tying flowers to the fence. Baboons from a different troop also gathered at the boundary, calling to the newly captive animals, the Daily Maverick reported.

“We stand together for the Seaforth and Waterfall troops, for their freedom, their dignity and their right to live as wild animals,” Mandy Neal, the administrator of the Save Kogelfontein Baboons Facebook group, posted on Monday, calling for weekly Sunday silent protests. “ Our message is simple: CAPTIVITY IS NOT CONSERVATION.”

The City of Cape Town said in a statement on Sunday that the relocation had been successful, with the baboons being monitored 24/7 after being checked by vets and the females receiving contraceptive implants.

It said: “The Waterfall troop has been relocated due to the severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment, the limited available natural low-lying habitat, the increasing risk to the baboons’ welfare, and public safety concerns … [and] as a very last resort after other interventions were evaluated and deemed ineffective, and as an alternative to culling.”

Prof Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town, said the baboon management plan had undergone two years of public consultations. “It has thus been disappointing watching members of the public and select NGOs, many which did not engage in the stakeholder process, now compromising the safety and welfare of the baboons and people through violent actions directed at staff and baboons in transit.”

articles.title: Monday briefing: The many stages of the UK-EU relationship – and what’s next
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: From situationship to a possible makeup, a look at the evolving relationship, and the bloc’s big feelings about the future
body: Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU summit this Friday, Andy Burnham is expected to make the reset of our relationship with Europe the pivotal theme of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet in London tonight.

The prospect of closer ties – and the possibility of going “all the way” to reversing Brexit – has been met with jubilation and relief in some quarters and vehement opposition in others, while around Westminster and across the media the psychodrama has been spiralling for weeks.

At this point, I’m reminded of that Robert Burns couplet: “O wad some Pow’r the giftie gie us / To see oursels as ithers see us!” What does the EU think about all this? Are they ready to reverse what leading figures have repeatedly described as a colossal act of self-harm? Or are they viewing this latest iteration with bombastic side-eye? I posed these questions to Jennifer Rankin, the Guardian’s Brussels correspondent. First the headlines.

UK news | A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent, which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds.

Youth unemployment | Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”.

Environment | The strongest El Niño in centuries has added urgency to UN climate talks in Turkey as vulnerable countries face “compounding” crises. In other Cop31 news, queer and gay protesters defied a crackdown on LGBTQ+ rights in Turkey to lead a civil society climate march.

UK news | Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police. West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested and appealed for witnesses to come forward.

Air transport | The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or cancelled thousands of flight stemmed from routine maintenance. The US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, blamed prior presidents and Congress for the stoppage.

Ahead of the summit, the pro-Brexit polity has been in broadcast mode: headlines from the past few days include: “Burnham’s plot to rejoin the EU would leave the average UK household £6,500 poorer” (Express); “Taxpayers funding pro-EU university courses” (Sunday Telegraph); “Staggering cost of PM’s EU reset” (Daily Mail).

Stay Out, a new campaign against rejoining the European Union, launched last week. While the guy you really want to hear from right now – David Cameron, the prime minister who lost the 2016 Brexit referendum – has insisted the UK’s problems have nothing to do with its exit from the EU.
Even within the Labour fold, there are rumblings of unease from MPs and unions.

But the one-day summit in Brussels this Friday does not include any formal discussion of rejoining: instead, the EU and UK hope to sign deals on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth experience scheme (a work and study exchange programme).

Still, the mood music is upbeat. Back in September, when Burnham first opened the door to a Brexit reversal, French president Emmanual Macron responded: “welcome back.” while Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez said: “Spain would welcome Britain’s return with open arms.”

The enthusiasm is genuine, says Jennifer. Indeed, some European diplomats have told her the technicalities could be wrapped up within a year because the UK remains closely aligned with the bloc in so many areas. “It would be such a vote of confidence in the European project for a country to decide to return after voting to leave”.
Situationship: what’s at stake at this week’s summit?

Though Burnham has predicted “some long nights” of negotiation this week, Jennifer says there’s optimism on each side as the first two deals on food and drink and emissions trading were largely agreed.

There are two sticking points with the youth exchange deal. First, the Home Office wants to limit numbers to the UK to keep migration figures low. Second, there’s disagreement over whether those students would pay UK domestic rates of tuition fees or the international rate, which is four or five times higher for some courses.

The UK is offering concessions on tuition fees if it can join Made in Europe, the EU legislation designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition. But the EU says it can’t make a deal on Made in Europe this week, because the law is still at a draft stage.

And here’s where it gets complicated. The European Commission has proposed delaying an agreement on tuition fees for six months, which could allow time to get the UK into Made in Europe, a diplomatic win for Britain. But there’s pushback from member states who want to pin down the UK on tuition fees this week. “This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms,” Jennifer says. “Lots of EU officials and diplomats studied in the UK, or their children did, and they felt this was one of the big losses of Brexit, that these person-to-person links were being eroded.”
On-again, off-again: what else could get in the way of closer working?

In play at Friday’s summit will also be a future deal on Britain’s return to the EU’s internal electricity market and a joint migration pact, with the UK pushing for access to EU crime databases to tackle the small boats crisis.

Member states are already working hard to smooth things out on the electricity front, to stop it becoming a sticking point. A couple of weeks ago, Jennifer reported on leaders from Germany, Denmark and elsewhere calling for deeper cooperation on clean energy – which she reads as an attempt to head off a row about how much the UK should contribute to EU cohesion funds for the evident privilege of cutting red tape, easing trade and, ultimately, reducing costs.
A similar row over UK contributions scuppered negotiations last year on our entry into a €150bn EU defence fund.

It could also be a challenge for the UK to realign with the EU on farming, after changing to a payment model that puts more emphasis on delivering environmental benefits. And past UK governments have been lukewarm about EU AI regulation, devised post Brexit.
Conscious partnership: will the EU welcome future closeness this week?

I learned long ago there’s no such thing as a stupid question, so I ask mine now: will there be a moment on Friday when Ursula von der Leyen offers the equivalent of Macron’s “welcome back”? Will there be a “just give us six months to sort out the paperwork Andy” vibe?

The European Commission president is, by nature, a cautious politician, Jennifer tells me, so she doesn’t expect anything so specific. “I’m sure she – and António Costa, the European Council president – will get asked about it at the press conference, and they’ll want to send a signal about the UK being welcome to rejoin.”

But behind closed doors, in Brussels and other capitals, what Jennifer hears repeatedly is that it’s up to the UK to decide what it wants. And, while the prospect of Brexiteer Nigel Farage in Downing Street has faded in recent months, there remains a deal of caution about the vicissitudes of UK politics. “Now the Burnham government is exploring the options, but there’s also an awareness that you could have a very different government in a few years’ time,” she says.
It’s not you, it’s me: what else is Europe worrying about?

The EU and its member states are preoccupied with far weightier problems: the war in Ukraine (Volodymyr Zelenskyy attends every EU summit), the rise in support for the far right, street protests, hybrid threats from Russia, a trade deficit with China that has reached a staggering €1bn a day in 2026.
“There are so many other issues crowding on the agenda,” says Jennifer. So it’s not all about us? “That’s actually been the theme of my decade of reporting from Brussels,” she says with a laugh.

There’s profound concern about the prospect of Marine Le Pen winning the French presidential elections next year, which could tip the bloc into a crisis if she pursues her resolutely anti-EU agenda, which includes reducing France’s substantial contribution to the EU budget.

Beyond that, there’s a broader question about increasingly divided and unstable politics across member states. “Every single member state has to agree to the UK’s re-entry,” Jennifer reminds me. “Who knows what the EU will look like in 2030 when Britain could be having a rejoin referendum?”

Some travellers seek out ancient landmarks when they visit a new place. Hidde Burgmans, from the Netherlands, looks for ancient trees – and he’s created an app of the same name to help people find remarkable old trees around the world, from Malaysian baobabs to the Fortingall yew in Perthshire, Scotland, thought to be an astounding 5,000 years old.

Users can review remarkable old trees around the world, and upload their favourites to the Ancient Trees app. “On Tuesday somebody photographed a tree in Edinburgh.
